## Overview

The previous vignettes build a generation by composing the kernel's operators directly.
Here the life cycle is written once, as syntax: a morphism of a free symmetric monoidal
category whose objects are the stages of a generation and whose generating morphisms
are the steps between them. A functor out of a free category is fixed by where it sends
the generators, so giving each step a meaning in a backend gives every life cycle built from
those steps a meaning there. Two such functors lower the life cycle: one to the
simulation kernel and one to Eidos, the scripting language of the population-genetics
simulator SLiM [@Haller2023].

The SLiM model lowered from QTSim's life cycle is, run for run, the SLiM port of QTSim
that was written by hand for this project, and it agrees with QTSim in distribution,
with one locus or a hundred. A new step, given a meaning in both backends, yields two
simulators of a model QTSim does not have, which can be checked against each other: a
fluctuating optimum, and demes coupled by migration, which the monoidal product `⊗`
places side by side.

The vignette needs SLiM (version 4 or later), the hand-written port and QTSim. It looks
for SLiM in `slim/build/slim` in the folder that holds the package's folder (the `SLIM`
environment variable, or a `slim` on the path, can stand in for it), takes the port from
the package's `validate/slim/qtsim.slim`, and looks for QTSim built from the source that
comes with the package (`make -C reference/QTSim`) or in the paper's code.

## Setup

```{julia}
using QTLSim
import Catlab                       # loads QTLSim's categorical layer
using Catlab: ⋅, ⊗, dom, codom, Hom
using CairoMakie, HypothesisTests, Printf, Random, Statistics
CairoMakie.activate!(type = "png")

const ROOT = normpath(joinpath(@__DIR__, "..", "..", ".."))
const SLIM = let built = joinpath(ROOT, "slim", "build", "slim")
    haskey(ENV, "SLIM") ? ENV["SLIM"] : isfile(built) ? built : something(Sys.which("slim"), built)
end
const PORT = joinpath(@__DIR__, "..", "..", "validate", "slim", "qtsim.slim")
include(joinpath(@__DIR__, "..", "..", "validate", "qtsim.jl"))   # find_qtsim(): see reference/QTSim/README.md
const QTSIM = something(find_qtsim(), "")
all(isfile, (SLIM, PORT, QTSIM)) || error("this vignette needs SLiM, the SLiM port and QTSim")
Threads.nthreads()
```

## The life cycle as a morphism

`lifecycle()` returns the syntax: the Catlab presentation of a free symmetric monoidal
category with four
objects, the stages of a generation, and seven generating morphisms, the steps of
QTSim's generation loop.

```{julia}
#| output: asis
L = lifecycle()
const STEP_NAMES = (:develop, :select, :reproduce, :record, :rescale, :mutate, :swap)
println("| step | from | to |\n|:--|:--|:--|")
for s in STEP_NAMES
    f = getfield(L, s)
    println("| `", s, "` | ", dom(f), " | ", codom(f), " |")
end
```

Steps compose with Catlab's `⋅` when the stage one step ends in is the stage the next
begins with. QTSim's generation is the composite of all seven, in the order of its loop,
and is a morphism from zygotes to zygotes:

```{julia}
(; develop, select, reproduce, record, rescale, mutate, swap) = L
qtsim = develop ⋅ select ⋅ reproduce ⋅ record ⋅ rescale ⋅ mutate ⋅ swap
```

Steps whose stages do not match do not compose. Selecting before developing is not a
life cycle, and Catlab says so:

```{julia}
try
    select ⋅ develop
catch e
    println(first(sprint(showerror, e), 120), "…")
end
```

## Two functors

`lower(f, :kernel)` sends each step to the kernel function it wraps (`develop!`,
`select!`, `reproduce!`, recording, the scheduled change of the fitness width,
`mutate!`, and the swap of the parent and offspring buffers), and composition to `⋅`.
The image of the generation is an operator on a `World`:

```{julia}
lower(qtsim, :kernel)
```

Run once per generation by `run_composed`, it is `run!`, bit for bit, here for one
locus, with the optimum moving from generation 5000 and the fitness function narrowing:

```{julia}
p = Params(PopSize = 1000, NoQTL = 1, Ploidy = 2, NoGenerations = 6500, PhenotypeVar = 0.02,
           Heritability = 0.5, MutationScalar = 0.001, MutationRatePerGamete = 0.0002,
           MoveFitnessSDGen = 5000, MoveFitnessSD = 1.0, MoveType = :phenotype,
           ChangeFitnessGen = 5000, ChangeFitnessSD = 0.3)
a = run!(World(p), Xoshiro(1))
b = run_composed(World(p), Xoshiro(1); cycle = qtsim)
all(getfield(a, k) == getfield(b, k) for k in keys(a))
```

`lower(f, :eidos)` sends each step to a fragment of Eidos. Each individual carries its
two allele values, as in QTSim's continuum-of-alleles model, and SLiM supplies only the
life cycle of a non-Wright–Fisher model. Selection, for example:

```{julia}
lower(select, :eidos)
```

Composition goes to concatenation, so the image of the generation is the seven
fragments in order:

```{julia}
lower(qtsim, :eidos).code == join(lower(getfield(L, s), :eidos).code for s in STEP_NAMES)
```

## A SLiM model from the life cycle

`slim_script` puts the image of a life cycle inside a complete SLiM model, in a
`reproduction()` callback that runs once per tick, with the parameters of a `Params` as
defaults that `slim -d` can override:

```{julia}
script = slim_script(qtsim, p)
print(script)
```

`run_slim` runs a SLiM model and reads the table it prints, which has the columns
QTSim's output has.

```{julia}
function run_slim(model, seed; defines = Dict{String,Any}())
    args = ["-s", string(seed)]
    for (k, v) in defines
        push!(args, "-d", v isa AbstractString ? "$k=\"$v\"" : "$k=$v")
    end
    path = tempname() * ".slim"; write(path, model)
    text = try read(`$SLIM $args $path`, String) finally rm(path; force = true) end
    rows = [split(l, '\t') for l in split(text, '\n') if occursin(r"^\d+\t", l)]
    (; gen = [parse(Int, r[1]) for r in rows], pheno_mean = [parse(Float64, r[2]) for r in rows],
       geno_var = [parse(Float64, r[3]) for r in rows], nsurv = [parse(Int, r[4]) for r in rows],
       theta = [parse(Float64, r[5]) for r in rows], extinct = occursin("Pop all died.", text),
       lines = [join(r, '\t') for r in rows])
end
nothing
```

## The generated model is the hand-written port

The package also has a SLiM port of QTSim written by hand, `validate/slim/qtsim.slim`,
validated against QTSim before the life cycle existed. Run with the same seed and
parameters, the generated model and the port print the same table, number for number,
because their steps are the same Eidos statements in the same order and so draw the same
random numbers. The one difference is intended: when a population dies, the port also
prints the generation in which it died, and QTSim does not.

```{julia}
#| output: asis
port = read(PORT, String)
checks = (
    ("stabilising selection", Dict{String,Any}("N" => 1000, "VP" => 0.02, "h2" => 0.5, "m" => 0.02,
        "rate" => 0.5, "NGEN" => 600, "moveGen" => -1, "changeGen" => -1, "changeSD" => -1.0, "initOmega" => 0.3)),
    ("moving optimum", Dict{String,Any}("N" => 1000, "VP" => 0.02, "h2" => 0.5, "m" => 0.001,
        "rate" => 0.0002, "NGEN" => 600, "moveGen" => 300, "moveSD" => 1.0, "changeGen" => 300,
        "changeSD" => 0.3, "initOmega" => -1.0)),
    ("extinction", Dict{String,Any}("N" => 300, "VP" => 0.02, "h2" => 0.5, "m" => 0.001,
        "rate" => 0.0002, "NGEN" => 600, "moveGen" => 50, "moveSD" => 6.0, "changeGen" => 50,
        "changeSD" => 0.05, "initOmega" => -1.0)))
println("| scenario | seeds | identical tables | extinct |\n|:--|--:|--:|--:|")
for (name, d) in checks
    same = Threads.Atomic{Int}(0); died = Threads.Atomic{Int}(0)
    Threads.@threads for seed in 1:10
        a = run_slim(port, seed; defines = d); b = run_slim(script, seed; defines = d)
        ref = a.extinct ? a.lines[1:end-1] : a.lines      # the port's extra line at extinction
        Threads.atomic_add!(same, Int(a.extinct == b.extinct && ref == b.lines))
        Threads.atomic_add!(died, Int(b.extinct))
    end
    println("| ", name, " | 10 | ", same[], " | ", died[], " |")
end
```

## The generated model agrees with QTSim

SLiM and QTSim draw different random numbers, so they can agree only in distribution.
Each of three scenarios is run 50 times by QTSim, by the SLiM model generated from the
life cycle, and by the kernel's image of the same life cycle. Scenarios A and B are those
of [Validation against QTSim](../08_validation_against_qtsim/08_validation_against_qtsim.qmd):
a sharp mutation–selection balance, and an optimum that keeps a fixed lead over the mean
phenotype from generation 5000 while the fitness function narrows. In scenario C the
optimum moves by a fixed amount each generation from generation 5000, as in the paper's
simulations. The hand-written port has no continuous move; the generated model has it
because the selection step does.

```{julia}
scen = (
    A = Params(PopSize = 1000, NoQTL = 1, Ploidy = 2, NoGenerations = 4000, PhenotypeVar = 0.02,
               Heritability = 0.5, MutationScalar = 0.02, MutationRatePerGamete = 0.5, InitFitnessSD = 0.3),
    B = p,
    C = Params(p; MoveType = :continuous, MoveFitnessSD = 0.002, ChangeFitnessGen = -1))

function write_qtsim_options(path, q::Params, seed)
    open(path, "w") do io
        println(io, "Sample $(q.Sample)\nPopSize $(q.PopSize)\nNoQTL $(q.NoQTL)")
        println(io, "Generations $(q.NoGenerations)\nPloidy $(q.Ploidy)")
        q.MoveFitnessSDGen != -1 && println(io, "MoveFitnessSD $(q.MoveFitnessSDGen) $(q.MoveFitnessSD)")
        q.ChangeFitnessGen != -1 && println(io, "ChangeFitnessSD $(q.ChangeFitnessGen) $(q.ChangeFitnessSD)")
        println(io, "OptimumMoveType $(q.MoveType)\nPhenotypeVar $(q.PhenotypeVar)")
        println(io, "MutationScalar $(q.MutationScalar)\nHeritability $(q.Heritability)")
        println(io, "MutationRatePerGamete $(q.MutationRatePerGamete)")
        q.NoQTL > 1 && println(io, "RecombinationPoissonMean $(q.RecombPoissonMean)")
        q.InitFitnessSD >= 0 && println(io, "InitFitnessSD $(q.InitFitnessSD)")
        println(io, "Seed $seed")
    end
end

function run_qtsim(q::Params, seed)
    opts = tempname() * ".txt"; write_qtsim_options(opts, q, seed)
    text = try read(`$QTSIM $opts`, String) finally rm(opts; force = true) end
    gen = Int[]; zbar = Float64[]; vg = Float64[]; ns = Int[]; θ = Float64[]; inbody = false
    for line in split(text, '\n')
        startswith(line, "Pop all died") &&
            return (; gen, pheno_mean = zbar, geno_var = vg, nsurv = ns, theta = θ, extinct = true)
        startswith(line, "Generation\t") && (inbody = true; continue)
        (inbody && !isempty(strip(line))) || continue
        f = split(line, '\t')
        push!(gen, parse(Int, f[1])); push!(zbar, parse(Float64, f[2])); push!(vg, parse(Float64, f[4]))
        push!(ns, parse(Int, f[5])); push!(θ, parse(Float64, f[6]))
    end
    (; gen, pheno_mean = zbar, geno_var = vg, nsurv = ns, theta = θ, extinct = false)
end

const R = 50
programs = (:QTSim, :SLiM, :kernel)
models = map(q -> slim_script(qtsim, q), scen)
jobs = [(prog, s, k) for prog in programs for s in keys(scen) for k in 1:R]
runs = Vector{Any}(undef, length(jobs))
Threads.@threads :greedy for j in eachindex(jobs)
    prog, s, k = jobs[j]
    q = scen[s]
    runs[j] = prog === :QTSim ? run_qtsim(q, 1000k) :
              prog === :SLiM ? run_slim(models[s], 1000k + 1) :
              run_composed(World(q), Xoshiro(1000k + 2); cycle = qtsim)
end
result(prog, s) = [runs[j] for j in eachindex(jobs) if jobs[j][1] === prog && jobs[j][2] === s]
nothing
```

The summary statistics are those of the validation vignette: the genetic variance at
equilibrium or at the end, the fraction of each generation that survives selection after
the move, and how far the mean phenotype advances. The table gives their medians over the
runs, and the p-values of two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov tests against QTSim.

```{julia}
#| output: asis
window(r, lo, hi) = findall(g -> lo <= g <= hi, r.gen)
statistics = (
    (:A, "equilibrium genetic variance", r -> mean(r.geno_var[window(r, 3000, 3999)])),
    (:B, "genetic variance at the end", r -> mean(r.geno_var[window(r, 6400, 6499)])),
    (:B, "survival after the move", r -> mean(r.nsurv[window(r, 5000, 6499)]) / 1000),
    (:B, "advance of the mean phenotype", r -> mean(r.pheno_mean[window(r, 6400, 6499)]) - mean(r.pheno_mean[window(r, 5000, 5010)])),
    (:C, "genetic variance at the end", r -> mean(r.geno_var[window(r, 6400, 6499)])),
    (:C, "survival after the move", r -> mean(r.nsurv[window(r, 5000, 6499)]) / 1000),
    (:C, "advance of the mean phenotype", r -> mean(r.pheno_mean[window(r, 6400, 6499)]) - mean(r.pheno_mean[window(r, 5000, 5010)])))
ksp(a, b) = pvalue(ApproximateTwoSampleKSTest(a, b))
println("| scenario | statistic | QTSim | SLiM (generated) | kernel | KS p, SLiM | KS p, kernel |")
println("|:--|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|")
for (s, name, f) in statistics
    v = Dict(prog => [f(r) for r in result(prog, s) if !r.extinct] for prog in programs)
    @printf("| %s | %s | %.4g | %.4g | %.4g | %.2f | %.2f |\n", s, name,
            median(v[:QTSim]), median(v[:SLiM]), median(v[:kernel]), ksp(v[:SLiM], v[:QTSim]), ksp(v[:kernel], v[:QTSim]))
end
@printf("\nExtinctions: %s.\n", join(("$prog $(sum(r.extinct for s in keys(scen) for r in result(prog, s)))" for prog in programs), ", "))
```

Twelve of the fourteen comparisons are comfortably consistent. The two below 0.05 are
both for the SLiM model in scenario B: the genetic variance at the end of the run and the
advance of the mean phenotype, which depends on it. With fourteen tests one or two such
p-values are not unusual, and these are the noisiest statistics here: in scenario B about
0.4 new mutations enter the population each generation, each with a standard deviation of
0.16, more than the phenotypic standard deviation of 0.14, so the genetic variance late
in a run rests on a handful of them. Ten times as many runs of scenario B, with new
seeds, settle it:

```{julia}
#| output: asis
const RB = 500
jobs_b = [(prog, k) for prog in programs for k in 1:RB]
runs_b = Vector{Any}(undef, length(jobs_b))
Threads.@threads :greedy for j in eachindex(jobs_b)
    prog, k = jobs_b[j]
    runs_b[j] = prog === :QTSim ? run_qtsim(scen.B, 170_000 + k) :
                prog === :SLiM ? run_slim(models.B, 180_000 + k) :
                run_composed(World(scen.B), Xoshiro(190_000 + k); cycle = qtsim)
end
println("| scenario B, $RB runs each | QTSim | SLiM (generated) | kernel | KS p, SLiM | KS p, kernel |")
println("|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|")
for (s, name, f) in statistics
    s === :B || continue
    v = Dict(prog => [f(runs_b[j]) for j in eachindex(jobs_b) if jobs_b[j][1] === prog && !runs_b[j].extinct]
             for prog in programs)
    @printf("| %s | %.4g | %.4g | %.4g | %.2f | %.2f |\n", name, median(v[:QTSim]), median(v[:SLiM]),
            median(v[:kernel]), ksp(v[:SLiM], v[:QTSim]), ksp(v[:kernel], v[:QTSim]))
end
```

With ten times the runs nothing separates the three programs: the two low p-values
were chance.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-lag
#| fig-cap: "Scenario C: how far the mean phenotype lags behind the optimum after the optimum starts to move at generation 5000, averaged over the 50 runs of each program."
fig = Figure(size = (720, 380))
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1], xlabel = "generation", ylabel = "lag of the mean phenotype, θ − z̄")
for (prog, c) in zip(programs, (:gray30, :crimson, :navy))
    rs = filter(r -> !r.extinct, result(prog, :C))
    @assert all(r -> r.gen == 0:6499, rs)                # one row per generation
    gens = 4900:6499
    lag = [mean(r.theta[g + 1] - r.pheno_mean[g + 1] for r in rs) for g in gens]
    lines!(ax, gens, lag, color = c, label = string(prog))
end
axislegend(ax, position = :lt)
fig
```

In scenario C the three programs' lag curves lie on top of one another: the mean
phenotype falls further and further behind the moving optimum, ever more slowly as
selection against the lag strengthens.

## A new step, lowered twice

A step that QTSim does not have, an optimum that fluctuates from generation to
generation, is a new generator: Catlab's `Hom` gives it a name and the stages it
connects, here adults to adults, between development and selection. A life cycle that
uses it type-checks like any other:

```{julia}
Adults = codom(develop)
fluctuate = Hom(:fluctuate, Adults, Adults)
noisy = develop ⋅ fluctuate ⋅ select ⋅ reproduce ⋅ record ⋅ rescale ⋅ mutate ⋅ swap
```

The lowering functors know nothing of `fluctuate`, so each needs its image: in the
kernel, a function that draws a new optimum; in Eidos, the statement that does the same.

```{julia}
σθ = 0.15
images = (kernel = Dict(:fluctuate => (w, rng) -> (w.θ = σθ * randn(rng); w)),
          eidos = Dict(:fluctuate => """
              // fluctuate: a new optimum each generation   [Adults → Adults]
              @POP@.setValue("THETA", rnorm(1, 0.0, $σθ));
          """))
noisy_model = slim_script(noisy, scen.A; images = images.eidos)
print(noisy_model[findfirst("// develop", noisy_model).start:findfirst("// reproduce", noisy_model).start-1])
```

With the optimum's standard deviation at 0.15, about one phenotypic standard deviation,
the two backends are two independent simulators of the new model. Each is run 50 times
under scenario A, with the constant optimum's runs from above for comparison (medians,
and the p-value of a Kolmogorov–Smirnov test between the backends):

```{julia}
#| output: asis
noisy_runs = Vector{Any}(undef, 2R)
Threads.@threads :greedy for j in 1:2R
    noisy_runs[j] = j <= R ? run_slim(noisy_model, 5000 + j) :
                    run_composed(World(scen.A), Xoshiro(5000 + j); cycle = noisy, images = images.kernel)
end
vg(r) = mean(r.geno_var[window(r, 3000, 3999)])
sv(r) = mean(r.nsurv[window(r, 3000, 3999)]) / 1000
println("| life cycle | statistic | SLiM | kernel | KS p |\n|:--|:--|--:|--:|--:|")
for (name, f) in (("equilibrium genetic variance", vg), ("survival", sv))
    for (cycle, sl, ke) in (("constant optimum", result(:SLiM, :A), result(:kernel, :A)),
                            ("fluctuating optimum", noisy_runs[1:R], noisy_runs[R+1:end]))
        xs = f.(sl); ys = f.(ke)
        @printf("| %s | %s | %.4g | %.4g | %.2f |\n", cycle, name, median(xs), median(ys), ksp(xs, ys))
    end
end
# Gaussian selection: E[W] = c ω / √(ω² + V_P + σθ²), with QTSim's c = 1/(0.4√(2π))
predicted(vgeq, σ2) = scen.A.InitFitnessSD / sqrt(scen.A.InitFitnessSD^2 + vgeq + envVar(scen.A) + σ2) /
                      (0.4 * sqrt(2π))
@printf("\nGaussian selection predicts survival %.3f with the constant optimum and %.3f with the fluctuating one, at the genetic variance the kernel's runs reach.\n",
        predicted(median(vg.(result(:kernel, :A))), 0.0), predicted(median(vg.(noisy_runs[R+1:end])), σθ^2))
```

The two backends agree with each other, and both match what Gaussian selection
predicts: a fluctuating optimum adds its variance to the spread of phenotypes about the
optimum, and so lowers survival.

## Many loci

The paper's simulations had 100 to 5000 loci. The Eidos images of `develop`,
`reproduce` and `mutate` handle any number: each individual carries its two chromosomes
as vectors of allele values, the genotype sums them, each gamete copies a parental
chromosome and switches strands at most once, as QTSim does, and each mutation lands on
a random locus. With one locus they reduce to the statements of the hand-written port,
which is why the comparison above still holds. Two scenarios with 100 loci, each run 50
times by QTSim, by the generated SLiM model and by the kernel: stabilising selection
(scenario D), and the optimum moving by 0.05 per generation from generation 1000, about
a third of a phenotypic standard deviation, until the population dies (scenario E).

```{julia}
#| output: asis
D = Params(PopSize = 1000, NoQTL = 100, RecombPoissonMean = 3.0, Ploidy = 2, NoGenerations = 2000,
           PhenotypeVar = 0.03, Heritability = 0.4, MutationScalar = 0.005, MutationRatePerGamete = 1e-4,
           InitFitnessSD = 4.0)
E = Params(D; RecombPoissonMean = 5.0, MoveFitnessSDGen = 1000, MoveFitnessSD = 0.05, MoveType = :continuous)
loci = (D = D, E = E)
loci_models = map(q -> slim_script(qtsim, q), loci)
jobs_l = [(prog, s, k) for prog in programs for s in keys(loci) for k in 1:R]
runs_l = Vector{Any}(undef, length(jobs_l))
Threads.@threads :greedy for j in eachindex(jobs_l)
    prog, s, k = jobs_l[j]
    q = loci[s]
    runs_l[j] = prog === :QTSim ? run_qtsim(q, 3000 + k) :
                prog === :SLiM ? run_slim(loci_models[s], 4000 + k) :
                run_composed(World(q), Xoshiro(5000 + k); cycle = qtsim)
end
result_l(prog, s) = [runs_l[j] for j in eachindex(jobs_l) if jobs_l[j][1] === prog && jobs_l[j][2] === s]
after_move(r) = (r.extinct ? last(r.gen) + 1 : 2000) - 1000     # no program prints the dying generation
println("| scenario | statistic | QTSim | SLiM (generated) | kernel | KS p, SLiM | KS p, kernel |")
println("|:--|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|")
for (s, name, f) in ((:D, "genetic variance, generations 1500–1999", r -> mean(r.geno_var[window(r, 1500, 1999)])),
                     (:D, "survival, generations 1500–1999", r -> mean(r.nsurv[window(r, 1500, 1999)]) / 1000),
                     (:E, "genetic variance before the move", r -> mean(r.geno_var[window(r, 900, 999)])),
                     (:E, "generations to extinction after the move", r -> Float64(after_move(r))))
    v = Dict(prog => [f(r) for r in result_l(prog, s)] for prog in programs)
    @printf("| %s | %s | %.4g | %.4g | %.4g | %.2f | %.2f |\n", s, name, median(v[:QTSim]), median(v[:SLiM]),
            median(v[:kernel]), ksp(v[:SLiM], v[:QTSim]), ksp(v[:kernel], v[:QTSim]))
end
@printf("\nExtinct in scenario E: %s.\n", join(("$prog $(count(r -> r.extinct, result_l(prog, :E)))/$R" for prog in programs), ", "))
```

With 100 loci the generated SLiM model agrees with QTSim: no statistic separates them.
One comparison of the kernel falls just below 0.05, its genetic variance in scenario D;
among eight tests that is not unusual, and the kernel's algorithm is QTSim's, as
[Validation against QTSim](../08_validation_against_qtsim/08_validation_against_qtsim.qmd)
checks bit for bit with QTSim's own random numbers.

## Demes and migration

The life cycle is a morphism of a free *symmetric monoidal* category: besides composing
steps in sequence with `⋅`, it places life cycles side by side with Catlab's `⊗`.
`qtsim ⊗ qtsim ⊗ qtsim` is three demes, each running QTSim's generation, from
`Zygotes⊗Zygotes⊗Zygotes` to itself, and `L.migrate(3)` is a new kind of step on such a
product: each offspring changes places, with a given probability, with an offspring of
another deme.

```{julia}
meta = qtsim ⊗ qtsim ⊗ qtsim ⋅ L.migrate(3)
```

Both functors preserve `⊗` as well as `⋅`. In the kernel, the image of a product acts on
each deme of a metapopulation (`p ⊗ demes(3)`) with the image of its factor, and the
image of `migrate` exchanges individuals between demes, so `run_composed` runs the
metapopulation. In Eidos, each factor's code runs in its own subpopulation, in a block
of its own that a deme's extinction leaves early, and migration acts on the offspring of
all three:

```{julia}
meta_script = slim_script(meta, p; migration_rate = 0.01)
print(meta_script[findfirst("    // migrate:", meta_script).start:findfirst("    dead = 0;", meta_script).start-1])
```

QTSim has no demes, so here the two backends check each other. With no selection
(`Drift = true`), the means of isolated demes drift apart, and migration holds them
together; three demes of 300 individuals with 10 loci each, for 500 generations, run 50
times by each backend at each of three migration rates:

```{julia}
#| output: asis
neutral = Params(PopSize = 300, NoQTL = 10, RecombPoissonMean = 1.0, Ploidy = 2, NoGenerations = 500,
                 PhenotypeVar = 0.02, Heritability = 0.5, MutationScalar = 0.02, MutationRatePerGamete = 0.01,
                 Drift = true)
rates = (0.0, 0.01, 0.1)
jobs_m = [(prog, m, k) for prog in (:SLiM, :kernel) for m in rates for k in 1:R]
runs_m = Vector{Any}(undef, length(jobs_m))
meta_models = Dict(m => slim_script(meta, neutral; migration_rate = m) for m in rates)
Threads.@threads :greedy for j in eachindex(jobs_m)
    prog, m, k = jobs_m[j]
    runs_m[j] = if prog === :SLiM
        r = run_slim(meta_models[m], 6000 + k)          # its rows end with the deme
        (; r.gen, r.pheno_mean, r.geno_var, deme = [parse(Int, split(l, '\t')[7]) for l in r.lines])
    else
        run_composed(neutral ⊗ demes(3), Xoshiro(7000 + k); cycle = meta, migration_rate = m)
    end
end
at_end(r, f) = [f(r)[(r.gen .== 499) .& (r.deme .== d)][1] for d in 1:3]
among(r) = var(at_end(r, x -> x.pheno_mean))          # variance among the three deme means
within(r) = mean(at_end(r, x -> x.geno_var))          # mean genetic variance within a deme
println("| migration rate | statistic | SLiM (generated) | kernel | KS p |\n|:--|:--|--:|--:|--:|")
for m in rates, (name, f) in (("variance among deme means", among), ("genetic variance within a deme", within))
    sl = [f(runs_m[j]) for j in eachindex(jobs_m) if jobs_m[j][1] === :SLiM && jobs_m[j][2] == m]
    ke = [f(runs_m[j]) for j in eachindex(jobs_m) if jobs_m[j][1] === :kernel && jobs_m[j][2] == m]
    @printf("| %g | %s | %.4g | %.4g | %.2f |\n", m, name, median(sl), median(ke), ksp(sl, ke))
end
```

The two backends agree at every migration rate: without migration the deme means
spread apart by drift, and migration at 1% or 10% per generation keeps them together
while raising the genetic variance within each deme, which now receives variation from
the others. `lean/CategoricalQuantGen/Demes.lean` proves the laws the metapopulation
relies on: running products step by step is running each deme on its own (the
interchange law, also for independent Markov kernels, so the order in which a backend
visits the demes does not matter), demes without migration iterate independently, and
migration, which only rearranges individuals among positions, keeps every deme's size
and every total over the metapopulation.

## Summary

QTSim's life cycle is written once, as the morphism
`develop ⋅ select ⋅ reproduce ⋅ record ⋅ rescale ⋅ mutate ⋅ swap` of a free symmetric
monoidal category, and two functors lower it: to the simulation kernel, where it is
`run!` bit for bit, and to Eidos, where it is the hand-written SLiM port run for run, in
agreement with QTSim in distribution, including the continuous move of the optimum and
the many loci that the port never had. A new step needs one image per backend and
nothing else, and the monoidal product turns one population into demes, which migration
couples, in both backends at once. That a lowering is fixed by its images on the steps,
and that for Markov kernels two lowerings whose steps agree in distribution give the
whole generation the same distribution, is proved in Lean in
`lean/CategoricalQuantGen/Lowering.lean`, and the laws of demes and migration in
`Demes.lean`.
